verdict.summary:
# WCAG 2.2 pointer-target size: direct answer

**Publication basis:** W3C *Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2*, W3C Recommendation (first published 5 October 2023; re-published as a Recommendation 12 December 2024 with editorial changes). The figures below are identical in both publications and in the WAI Understanding documents.

## 1. The Level AA criterion

**Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — Level AA — new in WCAG 2.2.**

It sits in Guideline 2.5 Input Modalities. Normative text (REC-WCAG22-20231005, §2.5.8):

> The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except where:
>
> **Spacing:** Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target;
> **Equivalent:** The function can be achieved through a different control on the same page that meets this criterion;
> **Inline:** The target is in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text;
> **User agent control:** The size of the target is determined by the user agent and is not modified by the author;
> **Essential:** A particular presentation of the target is essential or is legally required for the information being conveyed.

## 2. The Level AAA criterion

**Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) — Level AAA.** Normative text:

> The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels except when:
>
> **Equivalent** — the target is available through an equivalent link or control on the same page that is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels;
> **Inline** — the target is in a sentence or block of text;
> **User Agent Control** — the size of the target is determined by the user agent and is not modified by the author;
> **Essential** — a particular presentation of the target is essential to the information being conveyed.

## 3. Answer table

| Ask | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Constraint | WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, 5 Oct 2023; re-published 12 Dec 2024) |
| 2 | Level AA criterion that sets a minimum pointer-target size | **SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)** |
| 3 | That size, in CSS pixels | **at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels** (24 minimum) |
| 4 | Diameter of the circle used by its spacing exception | **24 CSS pixels** (a 24 CSS px diameter circle centered on the bounding box of each undersized target; the circles must not intersect another target or another undersized target's circle) |
| 5 | Larger size required by Level AAA Target Size (Enhanced), SC 2.5.5 | **at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels** (44 minimum) |

## 4. One-line version

> SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA, requires targets for pointer inputs to be at least **24 × 24 CSS pixels**; its spacing exception uses a **24 CSS-pixel-diameter circle** centered on the bounding box of each undersized target; the Level AAA SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) requires at least **44 × 44 CSS pixels**.

## 5. Precision notes (things that are commonly misquoted)

1. **"At least", not "exactly".** Both criteria are floors. A 60 × 60 target passes both the AA and AAA size requirement; a 30 × 30 target passes AA (and may pass AAA only via an exception) but not AAA's size requirement.
2. **The unit is CSS pixels**, not device/physical pixels — this is why the value scales with page zoom and with the CSS reference pixel, and why an implementation in `rem`/`em` is acceptable provided the computed size resolves to ≥ 24 × 24 CSS px (AAA: ≥ 44 × 44 CSS px).
3. **The AA spacing circle is 24 CSS px in diameter, not radius.** It is centered on the *bounding box* of each undersized target (i.e., centered on the box, not on the visual glyph or icon), and the test is that this circle must not intersect *another target* or *the circle of another undersized target*. The AAA criterion (2.5.5) has **no spacing exception at all** — its only size-relief exceptions are Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, and Essential.
4. **Size test is a contained square, per the Understanding document:** a target is "at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels" if a solid 24 × 24 CSS pixel square, axis-aligned to the page (the target itself may be rotated/skewed), can be drawn entirely within the target's area.
5. **Don't confuse 2.5.8 with 2.5.5.** 2.5.8 is the new-in-2.2 Level AA criterion (24 px); 2.5.5 is the pre-existing Level AAA criterion carried forward from WCAG 2.1 (44 px). Non-WCAG platform guidance (e.g., 44 pt on iOS, 48 dp on Android) is *not* what WCAG 2.2 AA requires; those figures are unrelated to the 2.5.8 threshold and must not be substituted for it.
6. **SC 2.5.8's exception list has five items** (Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User agent control, Essential); 2.5.5's has four (Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential). The AA "Inline" exception is conditioned on the target being in a sentence *or its size being constrained by the line-height of non-target text*, which is broader than AAA's plain "in a sentence or block of text".
7. **Version stability:** the 5 October 2023 Recommendation and the 12 December 2024 re-publication give identical numbers (24/24/44); the only changes in the later publication are editorial. No errata change these thresholds.

## 6. Sources

- WCAG 2.2 Recommendation, §2.5.5 and §2.5.8 — https://www.w3.org/TR/2023/REC-WCAG22-20231005/ and https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- Understanding SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum
- Understanding SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-enhanced.html
- WCAG 2.2 publication history — https://www.w3.org/standards/history/WCAG22/

findings.question:
1. A vendor questionnaire for the W3C web content accessibility Recommendation published in December 2024 (conformance target Level AA) asks for a pass or fail result on success criterion 4.1.1 'Parsing' (well-formed markup, unique IDs). Must a page pass 4.1.1 to conform to that version, and what does the document say is the reason?
2. Which WCAG version the December 2024 Recommendation is, and whether 4.1.1 is included, omitted, or explicitly removed in it — the pass/fail verdict and the cited reason both turn entirely on this.
3. The document's own normative statement of the reason (removal rationale or conformance clause), since the answer must quote that reason rather than supply an external justification.

5.2 Conformance Requirements
In order for a web page to conform to WCAG 2.2, all of the following conformance requirements must be satisfied:
5.2.1 Conformance Level
One of the following levels of conformance is met in full.
For Level A conformance (the minimum level of conformance), the web page
satisfies all the Level A success criteria, or a conforming alternate version is provided.
For Level AA conformance, the web page satisfies all the Level A and Level AA success criteria, or a Level AA conforming alternate version is provided.
For Level AAA conformance, the web page satisfies all the Level A, Level AA and Level AAA success criteria, or a Level AAA conforming alternate version is provided.
Note 1
Although conformance can only be achieved at the stated levels, authors are encouraged to report (in their claim) any progress toward meeting success criteria from all levels beyond the achieved level of conformance.
Note 2
It is not recommended that Level AAA conformance be required as a general policy for entire sites because it is not possible to satisfy all Level AAA success criteria for some content.

WCAG 3 Name
WCAG 2 and WCAG 3 have different names.
The new standard is currently referred to as “W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0”. This name was chosen because of wide-spread familiarity with the “WCAG” acronym, and to encompass the broader scope beyond “web content”.
How and why is WCAG 2 Success Criteria 4.1.1 Parsing obsolete?
Success Criteria 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete. WCAG 2.2 indicates it as 4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed), along with a note.
WCAG 2.1 and WCAG 2.0 now include this note from a conformance perspective:
This Success Criteria should be considered as always satisfied for any content using HTML or XML.
That note is in:
Updated WCAG 2.1 that includes new notes under 4.1.1 Parsing and incorporates errata listed in the WCAG 2.1 changelog
WCAG 2.0 errata
Understanding WCAG documents
Parsing was included in WCAG 2.0 to ensure that browsers and assistive technologies could accurately parse markup and content. Since then, specifications (such as HTML) and browsers have improved how they handle parsing errors. Also, previously assistive technology did their own markup parsing. Now they rely on the browser.

When a new version of WCAG 2 is published, does it change the previous version?

quotes.whole:
created according to the rules defined in the formal grammar for that technology.
In markup languages, errors in element and attribute syntax and
failure to provide properly nested start/end tags lead to errors that
prevent user agents from parsing the content reliably.
Therefore, the success criterion requires that the content can be parsed using only
the rules of the formal grammar.
Note
The concept of "well formed" is close to what is required here. However, exact parsing
requirements vary amongst markup languages, and most non XML-based languages do not
explicitly define requirements for well formedness. Therefore, it was necessary to
be more explicit in the success criterion in order to be generally applicable to markup
languages. Because the term "well formed" is only defined in XML, and (because end
tags are sometimes optional) valid HTML does not require well formed code, the term
is not used in this success criterion.

Additive, with one removal
WCAG 2.2 is an additive update. W3C states it “provides 9 additional success criteria since WCAG
2.1,” and that “the 2.0 and 2.1 success criteria are essentially the same in 2.2, with one
exception”
(Source:
W3C WAI, What's New in WCAG 2.2
)
.
The one exception is the removal of 4.1.1 Parsing. For the full list of the nine additions, see
what’s new in WCAG 2.2; for the side-by-side, see
WCAG 2.1 vs 2.2.
Why 4.1.1 Parsing was removed
4.1.1 Parsing (formerly Level A) is the only success criterion removed in WCAG 2.2. The note attached
to it in the Recommendation explains why:
WCAG 2.2 Recommendation, 4.1.1 (verbatim)

verdict.summary:
# Determination: SC 4.1.1 'Parsing' under the December 2024 W3C Recommendation, conformance target Level AA

## 0. Identify the document before answering (resolves the version ambiguity)

The request names the standard only by date. The December 2024 W3C Recommendation is **WCAG 2.2**, updated edition published **12 December 2024** (WCAG 2.2 was first published as a Recommendation on 5 October 2023; the 12 December 2024 edition is the current 'This version').

- Canonical URI: `https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/`
- Citation form to use on the questionnaire: *Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024, https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/*

Everything below is derived from that document; WCAG 2.0/2.1 are referenced only where WCAG 2.2 itself points back to them.

---

## 1. Ask 1 — Must a page pass 4.1.1 'Parsing' to conform to WCAG 2.2 at Level AA?

**Answer: No.**

### Normative basis

**(a) The criterion is not present as a requirement.** In WCAG 2.2 the entry reads **"4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed)"** — the heading itself carries the removal marker, and the entry consists of a note rather than a testable requirement. There is nothing in WCAG 2.2 that a page can pass or fail. Guideline 4.1 'Compatible' in 2.2 retains only 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value and 4.1.3 Status Messages.

**(b) The conformance clause only binds success criteria that exist.** WCAG 2.2 §5.2 Conformance Requirements:

> "In order for a web page to conform to WCAG 2.2, all of the following conformance requirements must be satisfied:"

§5.2.1 Conformance Level:

> "For Level AA conformance, the web page satisfies all the Level A and Level AA success criteria, or a Level AA conforming alternate version is provided."

Since 4.1.1 is no longer a success criterion in WCAG 2.2, it is not in the set that §5.2.1 requires. A page cannot be required to pass a criterion the version does not contain.

### Level does not change the answer

In the versions where it existed, **4.1.1 Parsing was Level A**, not Level AA. Because AA conformance requires all Level A *and* Level AA criteria (§5.2.1 above), 4.1.1 would have been in scope at an AA target had it survived. It did not survive, so the AA target is irrelevant to the outcome — the answer is the same at A, AA and AAA.

### What this means for the questionnaire

- **Do not answer "Fail" for 4.1.1 under any circumstances when the governing standard is WCAG 2.2.** A fail on a removed criterion produces a false non-conformance finding.
- **Preferred answer:** "Not Applicable — 4.1.1 was removed in WCAG 2.2 (Obsolete and removed)."
- **If the form forces a binary Pass/Fail:** answer **Pass**, with the qualifier "N/A — criterion removed in WCAG 2.2; conformance is not contingent on it." Do not leave it blank; blank fields are commonly scored as failures by questionnaire tooling.
- **Re-route real defects.** Genuine markup problems that would once have failed 4.1.1 are now assessed under **1.3.1 Info and Relationships** or **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value** (per W3C's own explanatory material). If the questionnaire has a free-text field, log them there. Removing 4.1.1 removes a duplicate check; it does not lower the bar.
- **Do not strike the row silently.** Record the N/A and the citation so an auditor can trace why the row is empty.

### Fallback if the questionnaire is actually governed by WCAG 2.1 (e.g. a legacy ACR/VPAT template)

If the governing version turns out to be WCAG 2.1 or 2.0 rather than 2.2, the answer is still never "Fail": the erratum note now carried in those documents states the criterion "should be considered as always satisfied for any content using HTML or XML." Answer "Pass (considered always satisfied — errata applied)" and reserve judgment only for non-HTML/XML markup languages.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — What does the document say is the reason?

**Reason identifier: `R-4.1.1-NO-UTILITY-REMOVED`**

### The document's own words (normative, WCAG 2.2 §4.1.1 note)

> "This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed."

— WCAG 2.2, §4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed), accompanying note.

**One-line statement of the reason (safe to paste):** *"This criterion no longer has utility and is removed."* — the stated grounds being that assistive technology no longer parses HTML directly, so the problems the criterion targeted either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria.

### Supporting explanation (informative, W3C-published — cite only as corroboration)

W3C WAI, *Understanding Success Criterion 4.1.1: Parsing (Obsolete and removed)*:

> "This criterion has been removed from WCAG 2.2. The intent of this success criterion was to ensure that user agents, including assistive technologies, can accurately interpret and parse content. Since WCAG 2.0 was published, the specifications (such as HTML) and browsers have improved their handling of parsing errors. It is also the case that assistive technology used to do their own parsing of markup, but now rely on the browser. For that reason this success criterion has been removed. Many issues that would have failed this criterion will fail Info and Relationships or Name, Role, Value."

W3C WAI, *WCAG 2 FAQ* ("How and why is WCAG 2 Success Criteria 4.1.1 Parsing obsolete?"):

> "Parsing was included in WCAG 2.0 to ensure that browsers and assistive technologies could accurately parse markup and content. Since then, specifications (such as HTML) and browsers have improved how they handle parsing errors. Also, previously assistive technology did their own markup parsing. Now they rely on the browser."

The FAQ also confirms the form of the entry in the Recommendation: "WCAG 2.2 indicates it as 4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed), along with a note."

### Normative vs informative — state this correctly

- The **requirement status** ("removed") and the **reason** are carried by the note under §4.1.1 of the Recommendation and by §5.2.1 of the Recommendation. Cite those.
- The Understanding document and the FAQ are **informative** W3C explanations. Use them to expand the rationale; do not present them as the normative source.
- Do **not** cite the third-party summary site (wcag22aa.org) or the WCAG2ICT meeting minutes as the authority. The minutes are a useful signal only: they record the working group's agreed wording, *"In WCAG 2.2, 4.1.1 Parsing was made obsolete and WCAG 2.2 removed it as a requirement, so this success criterion is not applicable"* — which independently corroborates the "not applicable" handling recommended above.

---

## 3. Questionnaire-ready answer block (copy as-is)

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Success criterion | 4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed) |
| Standard / version | WCAG 2.2, W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024, https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ |
| Conformance target | Level AA |
| Result | **Not Applicable** (if binary is required: **Pass — N/A, criterion removed**) |
| Must a page pass it to conform? | **No** |
| Reason (document's own words) | "This criterion no longer has utility and is removed." |
| Source | WCAG 2.2 §4.1.1 (note); conformance basis §5.2.1 |
| Notes | 4.1.1 was Level A in WCAG 2.0/2.1 and was removed in WCAG 2.2. Markup defects affecting accessibility are assessed under 1.3.1 Info and Relationships or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value. |

---

## 4. Evidence trail (for auditability)

1. `https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/` — §4.1.1 "Parsing (Obsolete and removed)" and its note; §5.2 and §5.2.1 Conformance Requirements. Normative.
2. `https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/faq/` — "How and why is WCAG 2 Success Criteria 4.1.1 Parsing obsolete?"; confirms the heading form and the 12 December 2024 update. Informative.
3. `https://w3c.github.io/wcag/understanding/parsing` — Understanding SC 4.1.1 (Obsolete and removed). Informative (editor's draft of the published Understanding doc).
4. `https://www.w3.org/2024/09/05-wcag2ict-minutes` — AG WG-adjacent resolution adopting "not applicable" wording for 2.2. Corroborative only.

## 5. Residual uncertainty

- The exact paragraph number of the note within §4.1.1 is not reproduced in the captured passages; cite it as "§4.1.1, accompanying note" rather than inventing a sub-number.
- If the questionnaire's governing version is disputed, the version statement in §0 (12 December 2024 edition of WCAG 2.2) is the fact to assert; the fallback in §1 covers a 2.1-governed form. In both cases the answer is never "Fail."

rounds is denoted by Nr, and the number of words of the key is denoted by Nk. (The number of
words in the state is denoted by Nb for Rijndael in general; in this Standard, Nb = 4.) The specifc
values of Nk, Nb, and Nr are given in Table 3; no other confgurations of Rijndael conform to
this Standard.

Key length Block size Number of rounds
Nk (in bits) Nb (in bits) Nr
AES-128 4 128 4 128 10
AES-192 6 192 4 128 12
AES-256 8 256 4 128 14
The three inputs to CIPHER() are: 1) the data input in, which is a block represented as a linear
array of 16 bytes; 2) the number of rounds Nr for the instance; and 3) the round keys. Thus,
AES-128(in,key) = CIPHER(in,10,KEYEXPANSION(key))
AES-192(in, key) = CIPHER(in,12,KEYEXPANSION(key))

1. Name of Standard. Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) (FIPS PUB 197).

cryptographic algorithm that can be used to protect electronic data. The AES algorithm is a
symmetric block cipher that can encrypt (encipher) and decrypt (decipher) information.
Encryption converts data to an unintelligible form called ciphertext; decrypting the ciphertext
converts the data back into its original form, called plaintext.
The AES algorithm is capable of using cryptographic keys of 128, 192, and 256 bits to encrypt
and decrypt data in blocks of 128 bits.

verdict.summary:
## AES-256 parameters per FIPS 197

### Answers

| Ask | Parameter | Value | Basis in FIPS 197 |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 2 | Number of rounds, Nr | **14** | Table 3 / Figure 4: AES-256 has Nk=8, Nb=4, Nr=14 |
| 3 | Block size | **128 bits** | Nb=4 words; word=32 bits; 4 x 32 = 128 bits |
| 4 | Four-word round keys consumed | **15** | Nr+1 = 15 AddRoundKey stages; key expansion gives 4(Nr+1)=60 words = 15 four-word round keys |

### Derivation

FIPS 197 Table 3, Key-Block-Round Combinations, lists AES-256 as:

- Nk = 8 words = 256-bit key
- Nb = 4 words = 128-bit block
- Nr = 14 rounds

FIPS 197 defines a word as a group of 32 bits. The block size is therefore Nb x 32 = 4 x 32 = **128 bits** (16 bytes). The 256 in AES-256 is the key length, not the block size.

For the round-key count, FIPS 197 Section 5.1 defines CIPHER as:

1. AddRoundKey with the first four-word key before any round.
2. Nr rounds, each ending with AddRoundKey.

That is Nr+1 = 14+1 = **15** AddRoundKey invocations, each consuming one four-word round key.

FIPS 197 Section 5.2 states that the key expansion produces 4(Nr+1) words. For AES-256:

4 x (14 + 1) = 60 words

Each round key is an array of four words, so:

60 / 4 = **15 round keys**

Equivalently: 15 round keys x 4 words x 32 bits = 1920 bits of expanded key, matching 4(Nr+1) x 32 = 60 x 32 = 1920 bits.

### Convention note

A count of 14 is sometimes reported when a source excludes the initial pre-round AddRoundKey and counts only the keys applied inside the 14 rounds. That is the value of Nr, not the number of four-word round keys consumed by the cipher. Under the FIPS 197 cipher definition, and under the question's wording, the cipher consumes **15** four-word round keys: w[0..3] for the initial AddRoundKey and w[4r..4r+3] for rounds r = 1 through 14.

### Grounding

- FIPS 197 (2001), Table 3 / Figure 4 and Sections 5.1-5.2.
- FIPS 197-upd1 (2023) retains the same technical values; NIST states the update makes no technical changes to the algorithm.
- The block size is 128 bits for AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256; AES-256 differs in key size, round count, and key-expansion recursion.

XAES-GCM: Uses a 12-byte random value to derive the AEAD key. The 12-byte random nonce 𝑁
is not used in the key derivation. The use of SP 800-108 reduces the length of the random value
compared to directly using AES-CMAC, but defining a general construction is appealing and could
be used also for Keccak- and Rijndael-256-based AEADs.
DNDK-GCM: Uses a 24-byte random value to derive the AEAD key and operates with a fixed
nonce. While AES-XGCM and XAES-GCM require 2–3 extra AES invocations per AES-GCM
invocation, DNDK-GCM requires 6 extra AES invocations. This is noticeable for short plaintexts
but negligible for longer plaintexts. The probability of collisions is the same as in XAES-GCM but
higher than AES-XGCM.
We think a function for deriving key-nonce pairs while keeping AES-GCM unchanged is a valuable
idea. While limiting the key length to 256 bits is acceptable, supporting multiple key lengths
appears straightforward. Key commitment is useful for specific applications but can be handled
through accordion modes.
None of AES-XGCM, DNDK-GCM, or XAES-GCM use AES-GCM with nonces longer than 96 bits.

IVs generated using the RBG-based construction
According to section 8.2.2, for IVs generated using the RBG-based construction, the random field (and
hence, the IV itself) must have length r ≥ 96 bits, and for any given IV length, the value r must be fixed for
the life of the key. Thus, for IVs generated using the RBG-based construction and where only one IV length
is allowed per key, one option is to limit the total number of IVs with a given key to 2s
, where
s = min((r-31)/2, 48.5).

For IVs generated using the deterministic construction and where only one IV length m is allowed per key,
one option is to impose no IV limit if m ≤ 128 (other than the constraints in section 8.3 on the invocation
and fixed fields of the IV), and to limit the total number of IVs with a given key to 248.5 if m > 128. For the

verdict.summary:
Answer (NIST SP 800-38D, November 2007, AES-GCM, RBG-based IV construction)

1) IV length: 96 bits (12 bytes).
- Sec. 5.2.1.1 sets the minimum IV length at 96 bits and states that, for interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design, implementations should restrict support to the length of 96 bits.
- Under the RBG-based construction (Sec. 8.2.2), IV = random field || free field, with random-field length r(i) >= 96 bits and r(i) fixed for the life of the key. Restricting the IV to 96 bits means the free field is empty (length 0) and the random field is 96 bits.
- So the recommended supported IV length is 96 bits = 12 bytes; longer IVs are permitted by the general minimum but are not the recommended restricted profile.

2) Maximum total invocations of the authenticated encryption function under one key: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 invocations.
- Sec. 8.3: the total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key.
- The only exception in Sec. 8.3 is for 96-bit IVs generated by the deterministic construction; that exception does not apply to RBG-based IVs. Therefore the RBG-based cap is 2^32.
- The Sec. 8.3 example of limiting each device to 2^20 invocations with 64-bit IVs, 2^21 with 96-bit IVs, and 2^20 with 128-bit IVs is an illustrative way to stay within the 2^32 per-key cap across devices; it is not a larger per-key allowance. A single key remains capped at 2^32 total authenticated-encryption invocations.

3) Maximum plaintext length per invocation: 2^39 - 256 bits = 2^36 - 32 bytes = 68,719,476,704 bytes.
- Sec. 5.2.1.1: the length of the plaintext shall not exceed 2^39 - 256 bits. This general GCM input-length restriction applies regardless of the IV construction, so it applies to RBG-based IVs.
- Conversion: (2^39 - 256)/8 = 2^36 - 32 bytes = 68,719,476,704 bytes = 64 GiB - 32 bytes.
- Equivalent block count: (2^32 - 2) 128-bit blocks = 4,294,967,294 blocks; 4,294,967,294 * 16 = 68,719,476,704 bytes. Do not round to 64 GiB exactly; the exact byte limit is 32 bytes less than 64 GiB.

4) Expressed in bytes (format): 68,719,476,704 bytes (2^36 - 32 bytes).

Scope notes:
- AES key size (128, 192, or 256 bits) does not change these figures.
- The 96-bit IV restriction is a 'should' recommendation; the 2^32 invocation cap and the 2^39 - 256 bit plaintext cap are 'shall not exceed' normative limits.
- The maximum plaintext length is per invocation; the 2^32 cap is per key across invocations.
- Source: NIST SP 800-38D, Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC, November 2007, Sec. 5.2.1.1, Sec. 8.2.2, Sec. 8.3.

This Recommendation specifies the Galois/Counter Mode (GCM), an algorithm for authenticated encryption with associated data, and its specialization, GMAC, for generating a message authentication code (MAC) on data that is not encrypted. GCM and GMAC are modes of operation for an underlying approved symmetric key block cipher.

Purge or wipe information from [ Assignment: organization-defined mobile devices ] based on [ Assignment: organization-defined purging or wiping requirements and techniques ] after [ Assignment: organization-defined number ] consecutive, unsuccessful device logon attempts.
Discussion: A mobile device is a computing device that has a small form factor such that it can be carried by a single individual; is designed to operate without a physical connection; possesses local, non-removable or removable data storage; and includes a self-contained power source. Purging or wiping the device applies only to mobile devices for which the organization-defined number of unsuccessful logons occurs. The logon is to the mobile device, not to any one account on the device. Successful logons to accounts on mobile devices reset the unsuccessful logon count to zero. Purging or wiping may be unnecessary if the information on the device is protected with sufficiently strong encryption mechanisms.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER (bottom line)

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, control AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) does NOT require a specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, a specific counting time period, or a specific lockout duration. All three are organization-defined assignment parameters. AC-7 is a parameteric control: its requirement is that the organization (1) sets the values and (2) enforces them. Any answer that quotes fixed numbers for AC-7 Rev.5 (e.g., 'three attempts in 15 minutes, 30-minute lockout') is not quoting AC-7.

1. CONTROL TEXT AS PUBLISHED (verbatim, both sources agree)

Source A — https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T12:07:01Z, sha256 fc63bcd61715):

  AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS
  Control:
  a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon
     attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
  b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment:
     organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an
     administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay
     algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined
     action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.

Source B — OSCAL-derived SP 800-53 v5.1 PDF, https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Projects/risk-management/800-53%20Downloads/800-53r5/SP_800-53_v5_1-derived-OSCAL.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T12:06:51Z, sha256 9ce01f4d67c9): identical wording ('organizaon-defined number', 'organizaon-defined me period', 'lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organzaon-defined me period]').

Corroborating: Rev.5 draft controls markup (sha256 8574eeabc495) and the bsafes mirror of the Rev.5 catalog (sha256 f9630cd5ebc4) reproduce the same three assignment slots.

2. MAPPING OF EACH ASK TO THE CONTROL TEXT

Askl 1 — number of consecutive invalid logon attempts
  Location: AC-7a. Text: 'Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user'.
  Fixed value in the control: none. The control publishes a slot, not a number. No lower or upper bound is stated anywhere in AC-7 (no 'at least', no 'no more than').

Askl 2 — time period over which attempts are counted
  Location: AC-7a. Text: '... during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.
  Fixed value in the control: none. AC-7 also does not state whether the window is sliding or fixed (a calendar day, a rolling 15 minutes, etc.) — that, too, is left to the organization's parameterization and implementation.

Askl 3 — lockout duration
  Location: AC-7b, first selection option. Text: 'lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.
  Fixed value in the control: none — and note the conditional structure: AC-7b is a Selection (one or more), so a lockout duration exists only if the organization selects the first option. The alternatives are:
    - lock the account or node until released by an administrator -> duration is indefinite, bounded only by administrative action (no parameter at all);
    - delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm] -> no lockout; a delay, governed by an organization-defined algorithm;
    - notify system administrator -> no lockout;
    - take other [Assignment: organization-defined action] -> organization-defined.
  So even the existence of a lockout duration is a selection choice, not a control mandate.

3. WHAT AC-7 DOES FIX (to confirm nothing numeric was missed)

- AC-7 Discussion (Source A): 'Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.' Even the prose points back to the organization-defined parameter; it recommends a shape (temporary, auto-releasing) but assigns no number.
- AC-7(1) Automatic Account Lock — '[Withdrawn: Incorporated into AC-7.]' (Source: bsafes mirror). The Rev.4 enhancement that carried lockout language is gone; nothing numeric survives it.
- AC-7(2) Purge or wipe mobile device — '[Assignment: organization-defined number]' consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts. Also organization-defined.
- AC-7(3) Biometric attempt limiting — 'Limit the number of unsuccessful biometric logon attempts to [Assignment: organization-defined number]'. Also organization-defined.
- AC-7(4) Use of alternate authentication factor — '(a) ... after the number of organization-defined consecutive invalid logon attempts have been exceeded; and (b) Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts through use of the alternative factors by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period].' Also organization-defined.
- Baselines (Appendix D, Table D-1): AC-7 appears in the LOW, MODERATE and HIGH baselines, with no AC-7 enhancements in any baseline. Baseline membership does not supply parameter values — it only means the (organization-defined) control must be implemented at all three impact levels.

Conclusion: there is no numeric literal anywhere in AC-7 Rev.5, base or enhancements.

4. FIGURES THAT CIRCULATE IN INDUSTRY AND ARE NOT AC-7 VALUES

A '3 attempts / 15 minutes / 30-minute lockout' triple is frequently attributed to 800-53. It does not appear in any AC-7 passage fetched from the publication, the OSCAL-derived edition, the Rev.5 draft markup, or the catalog mirror. Values of that kind come from organizational policy, agency/DoD-level instructions, vendor product defaults, or framework overlays — not from AC-7. Do not cite AC-7 as the source of such a number in an SSP, a control matrix, or an audit response; it will not survive a text check.

5. HOW THE VALUES GET SET (the work AC-7 actually demands)

Since AC-7 delegates the numbers, the deliverable an organization owes is a documented parameterization, recorded in the SSP/control implementation statement and traceable to the OSCAL parameters of control ac-7. Procedure:

Step 1 — Record the four/five parameter decisions explicitly:
  ac-7 parameter 1: number of consecutive invalid attempts (integer).
  ac-7 parameter 2: counting time period (duration + window semantics: sliding vs fixed).
  ac-7 parameter 3: lockout time period (duration) — only if AC-7b option 1 is selected.
  ac-7 parameter 4: delay algorithm (definition) — only if the delay option is selected.
  ac-7 parameter 5: 'other action' (definition) — only if that option is selected.
  (Parameter identifiers follow the OSCAL catalog's naming convention; confirm the exact IDs against the OSCAL copy of the catalog in use before pasting them into an automated artifact.)

Step 2 — Select AC-7b behavior per system/component and record which options were selected. Mixed selections are permitted by the control (e.g., lock the account, and notify the system administrator).

Step 3 — Justify the numbers against, at minimum: the authentication assurance level of the system (MFA vs password-only), the lockout-driven denial-of-service exposure (AC-7 Discussion explicitly flags this), whether AC-7(4) alternate factors or an administrative unlock path exists, and whether the same values must apply at the OS and application layers (the control's Discussion notes responses may be implemented at both).

Step 4 — Check for a binding overlays before finalizing: an agency security policy, a FedRAMP-style baseline package, or a system-specific overlays may fix values that AC-7 itself leaves open. If an overlays fixes them, cite the overlays, not AC-7, as the source.

Step 5 — Verify implementation matches the stated values: attempt counter resets on successful logon, the counter is per-user (AC-7a says 'by a user'), the window boundary behavior matches what was documented, and the lockout actually releases per the stated duration (or per administrator action if that option was chosen).

6. VERIFICATION ANY REVIEWER CAN REPEAT

- Grep the Rev.5 PDF for 'AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS' and read the block: the only bracketed items are the assignments quoted above.
- In the OSCAL catalog, resolve control id 'ac-7' and inspect its 'params' array — no value is populated in the catalog; values exist only in a profile or SSP.
- Grep the baselines table (Appendix D) for 'AC-7': it appears in LOW/MODERATE/HIGH with no enhancements, and no parameters.

7. SCOPE AND ROLE NOTE

This is a compliance-parameterization question, and the answer is a negative one about the publication: AC-7 Rev.5 mandates no number, no window, and no lockout duration. If what is actually needed is a defensible number for a specific system, that is a tailoring decision made under the organization's own risk acceptance, recorded as the AC-7 assignment values and traceable to whatever overlays imposes them — it cannot be sourced to AC-7 text.

Abstract
The protection of Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) is of paramount importance to
federal agencies and can directly impact the ability of the Federal Government to successfully
conduct its essential missions and functions. This publication provides federal agencies with
recommended security requirements for protecting the confidentiality of CUI when the
information is resident in nonfederal systems and organizations. The requirements apply to
components of nonfederal systems that process, store, or transmit CUI or that provide
protection for such components. The security requirements are intended for use by federal
agencies in contractual vehicles or other agreements established between those agencies and
nonfederal organizations. This publication can be used in conjunction with its companion

verdict.summary:
Compliance determination — NIST SP 800-171 security-requirement families and Rev. 2 status (retrieval date 2026-11-23).

1. Current revision and its family count
Current revision: NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Final, May 2024 (CSRC SP 800 listing shows `SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (Final)` dated `5/14/2024`, `Status: Final`). Rev. 2 is no longer current: NIST's Rev. 2 page states `Withdrawn on May 14, 2024. Superseded by SP 800-171 Rev. 3`.

Family count: 17 top-level security-requirement families.

Rev. 3 retains Rev. 2's 14 families and adds three families — Planning (PL), System and Services Acquisition (SA), and Supply Chain Risk Management (SR) — so 14 + 3 = 17. The 17-family set is: Access Control (AC), Awareness and Training (AT), Audit and Accountability (AU), Configuration Management (CM), Identification and Authentication (IA), Incident Response (IR), Maintenance (MA), Media Protection (MP), Personnel Security (PS), Physical and Environmental Protection (PE), Risk Assessment (RA), Security Assessment (CA), System and Communications Protection (SC), System and Information Integrity (SI), Supply Chain Risk Management (SR), Planning (PL), and System and Services Acquisition (SA). This is a count of families, not of individual requirements.

2. Revision 2's family count
14 top-level security-requirement families. Rev. 2's Chapter Three states: `This chapter describes fourteen families of recommended security requirements for protecting the confidentiality of CUI in nonfederal systems and organizations.` The 14 are: Access Control (AC), Awareness and Training (AT), Audit and Accountability (AU), Configuration Management (CM), Identification and Authentication (IA), Incident Response (IR), Maintenance (MA), Media Protection (MP), Personnel Security (PS), Physical and Environmental Protection (PE), Risk Assessment (RA), Security Assessment (CA), System and Communications Protection (SC), and System and Information Integrity (SI).

3. Revision 2's status on NIST's own published copy
NIST's Rev. 2 PDF carries a `Withdrawn Publication` sheet with `Withdrawal Date May 14, 2024` and the `Withdrawal Note`: `NIST SP 800-171r2 is withdrawn and superseded in its entirety by NIST SP 800-171r3`. NIST's CSRC Rev. 2 landing page uses the same status wording: `Withdrawn on May 14, 2024. Superseded by SP 800-171 Rev. 3`.

Therefore Rev. 2's status is: Withdrawn, with withdrawal date May 14, 2024, and superseded in its entirety by SP 800-171 Rev. 3. It is not the current revision.

Note: NIST's page for the Rev. 2 Initial Public Draft uses a different label — `Obsoleted on February 21, 2020 by SP 800-171 Rev. 2` — but that is the draft, not the final Rev. 2 publication addressed here.

Source record:
- Rev. 3 PDF: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-171r3.pdf
- Rev. 2 PDF: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-171r2.pdf
- NIST CSRC Rev. 2 page: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final
- NIST CSRC SP 800 list: https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/sp800

Bottom line: current revision = Rev. 3 with 17 families; Rev. 2 had 14 families; Rev. 2 is withdrawn on May 14, 2024 and superseded by Rev. 3.

quotes.whole:
By default, initdb uses the locale provider libc (see Section 23.1.4). The libc locale provider takes the locale settings from the environment, and determines the encoding from the locale settings.
To choose a different locale for the cluster, use the option --locale. There are also individual options --lc-* and --icu-locale (see below) to set values for the individual locale categories. Note that inconsistent settings for different locale categories can give nonsensical results, so this should be used with care.
Alternatively, initdb can use the ICU library to provide locale services by specifying --locale-provider=icu. The server must be built with ICU support. To choose the specific ICU locale ID to apply, use the option --icu-locale. Note that for implementation reasons and to support legacy code, initdb will still select and initialize libc locale settings when the ICU locale provider is used.
When initdb runs, it will print out the locale settings it has chosen. If you have complex requirements or specified multiple options, it is advisable to check that the result matches what was intended.
More details about locale settings can be found in Section 23.1.

Use checksums on data pages to help detect corruption by the I/O system that would otherwise be silent. This is enabled by default; use --no-data-checksums to disable checksums.

quotes.whole:
28.2.1. Off-line Enabling of Checksums
By default, data pages are protected by checksums, but this can optionally be disabled for a cluster. When enabled, each data page includes a checksum that is updated when the page is written and verified each time the page is read. Only data pages are protected by checksums; internal data structures and temporary files are not.
Checksums can be disabled when the cluster is initialized using initdb. They can also be enabled or disabled at a later time as an offline operation. Data checksums are enabled or disabled at the full cluster level, and cannot be specified individually for databases or tables.
The current state of checksums in the cluster can be verified by viewing the value of the read-only configuration variable data_checksums by issuing the command SHOW data_checksums.
When attempting to recover from page corruptions, it may be necessary to bypass the checksum protection. To do this, temporarily set the configuration parameter ignore_checksum_failure.
28.2.1. Off-line Enabling of Checksums #
The pg_checksums application can be used to enable or disable data checksums, as well as verify checksums, on an offline cluster.

quotes.whole:
Reverting to old cluster
If, after running pg_upgrade, you wish to revert to the old cluster, there are several options:
If the --check option was used, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.
If neither --link nor --swap was used, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.
If the --link option was used, the data files might be shared between the old and new cluster:
If pg_upgrade aborted before linking started, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.
If you did not start the new cluster, the old cluster was unmodified except that, when linking started, a .old suffix was appended to $PGDATA/global/pg_control. To reuse the old cluster, remove the .old suffix from $PGDATA/global/pg_control; you can then restart the old cluster.
If you did start the new cluster, it has written to shared files and it is unsafe to use the old cluster. The old cluster will need to be restored from backup in this case.
If the --swap option was used, the old cluster might be destructively modified:
If pg_upgrade aborts before reporting that the old cluster is no longer safe to start, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.

quotes.whole:
By default, initdb uses the locale provider libc (see Section 23.1.4). The libc locale provider takes the locale settings from the environment, and determines the encoding from the locale settings.
To choose a different locale for the cluster, use the option --locale. There are also individual options --lc-* and --icu-locale (see below) to set values for the individual locale categories. Note that inconsistent settings for different locale categories can give nonsensical results, so this should be used with care.
Alternatively, initdb can use the ICU library to provide locale services by specifying --locale-provider=icu. The server must be built with ICU support. To choose the specific ICU locale ID to apply, use the option --icu-locale. Note that for implementation reasons and to support legacy code, initdb will still select and initialize libc locale settings when the ICU locale provider is used.
When initdb runs, it will print out the locale settings it has chosen. If you have complex requirements or specified multiple options, it is advisable to check that the result matches what was intended.
More details about locale settings can be found in Section 23.1.

verdict.summary:
## 1. Verdict — are data checksums enabled?

**Yes. In PostgreSQL 18 a cluster created by `initdb` with no checksum-related option has data checksums ENABLED.**

This is a deliberate change of the default in the 18 release cycle (previously checksums were off unless you passed `-k`). PostgreSQL 18 release notes, incompatibilities section:

> "Change initdb default to enable data checksums (Greg Sabino Mullane). Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option --no-data-checksums. pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters."

And the `initdb` reference for `-k` / `--data-checksums`:

> "Use checksums on data pages to help detect corruption by the I/O system that would otherwise be silent. This is enabled by default; use --no-data-checksums to disable checksums."

So `-k` in PG18 is now a redundant no-op, and `pg_controldata` on a fresh default PG18 cluster reports a non-zero data page checksum version (1). Consequence to be aware of: the small CPU cost of computing/verifying a checksum per page write/read is now the default posture, and checksum failures are counted in `pg_stat_database.checksum_failures` / `checksum_last_failure`.

Verify the actual state rather than trusting the creation history (checksum state lives in `pg_control`):

```bash
# offline — works even if the cluster never started
pg_controldata "$PGDATA" | grep -i 'Data page checksum version'
#   'Data page checksum version: 1'  -> enabled
#   'Data page checksum version: 0'  -> disabled

# online
psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'      # on | off   (read-only GUC, cluster-wide)
```

`data_checksums` is set cluster-wide only; it cannot be set per database, per table, or per session, and it is not in `postgresql.conf`.

## 2. How checksums are switched off

There are exactly two supported ways, and **no SQL command that turns them off in place**. Per the docs: "Checksums can be disabled when the cluster is initialized using initdb. They can also be enabled or disabled at a later time as an offline operation. Data checksums are enabled or disabled at the full cluster level."

### Path A — at cluster creation (the cheap way)

```bash
initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data --no-data-checksums
# verify before first start
pg_controldata /var/lib/pgsql/18/data | grep -i 'Data page checksum version'   # -> 0
```

Use this for the new cluster in a `pg_upgrade` when the old cluster has no checksums (see §3). It costs nothing because the cluster is empty.

### Path B — on an existing cluster, offline, with `pg_checksums`

```bash
# 1. take a verified backup first (pg_basebackup or filesystem snapshot);
#    the tool rewrites every data page in the cluster.
# 2. clean shutdown — the tool refuses to run against a running server
pg_ctl -D "$PGDATA" stop -m fast

# 3. convert
pg_checksums --pgdata="$PGDATA" --no-checksums --progress --verbose
#    short forms: -D, -n/--no-checksums, -P, -v
#    to turn them back on later: pg_checksums -D "$PGDATA" --enable -P -v
#    to verify (only meaningful when enabled): pg_checksums -D "$PGDATA" --check -P

# 4. start and confirm
pg_ctl -D "$PGDATA" start
psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'      # -> off
```

Operational notes for Path B:

- Must run as the OS user that owns the data directory (same user as the server), with the server stopped; it will not run against a live cluster.
- It is a full-cluster page rewrite: size the maintenance window by data size and I/O throughput, and do not run it concurrently with anything else touching the data directory.
- If the cluster has physical standbys, plan the change for the whole replication set: checksum state is a `pg_control`-level property of each node, so every node must end up in the same state. Simplest safe procedure is to do the conversion with the replication topology quiesced (stop standbys, convert primary, convert each standby offline, restart).
- `--no-checksums` against a cluster that already has them off is a no-op; it reports the state and exits.
- If a run is interrupted, re-run it (and fall back to the backup if the cluster does not come up cleanly).

### What is NOT a way to switch them off

- No `ALTER SYSTEM` / `ALTER DATABASE` / `SET` — `data_checksums` is a read-only, preset GUC.
- `ignore_checksum_failure = on` does **not** disable checksums; it only makes the server tolerate (and warn about) a page that fails verification, for corruption-recovery purposes. It is a temporary read-time bypass, not a configuration change, and it does not stop checksums from being computed on write.

## 3. Constraint for `pg_upgrade` — the checksum settings must MATCH

**Rule: the old cluster and the new cluster must have the same data-checksum setting — both enabled or both disabled. `pg_upgrade` reads `pg_control` of both clusters (via `pg_controldata`) and aborts if the data page checksum versions differ.** This is stated explicitly in the PG18 release notes: "pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings."

The check happens during the compatibility check phase, before any file is copied/linked, so a mismatch aborts the upgrade without modifying either cluster (the exact fatal-message wording varies by version; the abort is on the `Data page checksum version` field of `pg_control`, so `pg_controldata` is the authoritative way to see what `pg_upgrade` will see).

### Pre-flight (do this before `initdb` on the new cluster)

```bash
# old cluster stopped:
pg_controldata /var/lib/pgsql/17/data | grep -i 'Data page checksum version'
# or, old cluster still running:
psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'

# new cluster (already initdb'ed, stopped):
pg_controldata /var/lib/pgsql/18/data | grep -i 'Data page checksum version'
```

### Decision matrix

| old cluster | `initdb` for the PG18 new cluster | upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| checksums ON (version 1) | `initdb -D $NEWDATA` (default = ON in 18) | OK |
| checksums ON (version 1) | `initdb -D $NEWDATA --no-data-checksums` | **aborts** |
| checksums OFF (version 0, typical pre-18) | `initdb -D $NEWDATA --no-data-checksums` | OK |
| checksums OFF (version 0) | `initdb -D $NEWDATA` (default ON in 18) | **aborts** |

This is precisely why the `--no-data-checksums` option was added in 18: upgrading a legacy non-checksum cluster now requires deliberately opting the new cluster out of the new default.

### Running the check step explicitly

```bash
# as the OS user owning both data directories; both servers stopped
pg_upgrade --check \
  --old-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/17/data --new-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/18/data \
  --old-bindir=/usr/pgsql-17/bin     --new-bindir=/usr/pgsql-18/bin
```

`--check` performs this and the other compatibility checks without touching data; always run it first.

### If you discover the mismatch after initdb

Cheapest fix is to convert the **new, still-empty** cluster, not the old one:

```bash
# new cluster stopped
pg_checksums -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data --no-checksums   # to match a non-checksum old cluster
# or
pg_checksums -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data --enable         # to match a checksummed old cluster
```

On an empty cluster this is near-instant. (Alternatively re-`initdb` with the correct flag; or, if you actually want checksums after the upgrade, upgrade with matching settings first and run `pg_checksums --enable` on the new cluster afterwards — that keeps `pg_upgrade` happy and still gets you checksums.)

### If you want to avoid the constraint entirely

Use a method that is not `pg_upgrade`: `pg_dumpall`/`pg_restore` or logical replication. Those move logical data, not pages, so the new cluster's checksum setting is free to differ from the old one.

## Assumptions made explicit

- Standard community PostgreSQL 18 behavior; a vendor build that overrides the `initdb` default would change the §1 verdict — verify with `pg_controldata` as shown rather than assuming.
- "Switched off" is read as both creation-time (`initdb --no-data-checksums`) and offline conversion (`pg_checksums --no-checksums`).
- The upgrade scenario assumes the old cluster is a pre-18 cluster (where the default was checksums off) — the case the release notes call out.
